The answer to Duty 1 ("where the 60 s goes") is only in the minion's chat reply: 4–13 ms per in-process item write, 4,816 ms for the first write over Servex HTTP, then 48 and 42 ms. No committed file has these numbers. `public/framework/ai/tracking/readme.md` (the new "JSONL read and write time" paragraph) should record them with the date, the branch and what each one measured (CLAUDE.md law 5).

The brief named three layers: (a) the item write path, (b) the page tail (`ext/JSONL` `live()`/follow) and (c) the browser loading a page.jsonl. `Server/JsonlPerf.mjs` times only (a), plus a raw read, parse and append. Layers (b) and (c) are not measured anywhere, and nothing in the report says they were skipped.

The in-process timing (`Server/JsonlPerf.mjs:52-69`, `run_item` imported straight from `Servex/agents/page_tools.js`) runs without the live Servex host around it. Locks, follow fan-out and index rebuilds may never fire, so 4–13 ms is a lower bound, not the real write cost. It was also run on the branch that already has the deputy's fix, not on the code that took 60 s. The page and readme present it as "the item tool's write time", and they should label it as a lower bound.

`Server/JsonlPerf.mjs:56` hard-codes the scratch path `sessions/2026/10/24/zz-jsonlperf-scratch-<pid>`, inside the real public tree. On any other day, `mkdirSync({recursive})` creates a `2026/10/24` folder that `rmSync` at line 68 never removes. The script also briefly writes inside the watched site tree, so Servex's file indexer may log the folder (this task's `page.jsonl` shows how it records files). Using `os.tmpdir()` with `TRACKING_ROOT`, or at least today's date, would be simpler and closer to the brief ("COPIES in os.tmpdir()").

`Server/TrackingCheck.mjs:144` calls `r.rid(p)` once per prompt. For a prompt without a cached id, `rid()` calls `this.rows()`, which reads and folds the whole `prompts.jsonl` again (`PromptRecords.mjs:111`). The check is quadratic per session. Reading the rows once and looking ids up by raw text would be cheaper.
`prompt_coverage()` and the read/parse half of `jsonl_perf()` now run on every `TrackingCheck` run, across every session folder and transcript. Nobody has timed how much slower this makes the report.

The two new page sections and the 5-column card row (`TrackingView.css`, `@container (min-width: 90em)`) were never opened in a browser: the minion says it ran only `node --check` and the CLI. This review came with no shots, so their layout is unchecked.

The readme (`public/framework/ai/tracking/readme.md`, last paragraph) and `Server/JsonlPerf.mjs:56` say the `--item` scratch copy can't go in `os.tmpdir()` because "run_item only writes under public/". That is false: `Servex/agents/page_tools.js:12` reads `SERVEX_PUBLIC` ("a test points the records at a scratch tree"). Set it to a `mkdtemp` folder before the dynamic import at `JsonlPerf.mjs:62`. That does what both briefs asked (os.tmpdir()), keeps the scratch copy out of the site tree, and makes the readme true.

Nothing in the readme or on the page says the bottom line of Duty 1: no measured layer came near 60 s. The worst was 4,816 ms, the cold first write over HTTP. Every number was taken on the branch that already has the deputy's fast write, so the 60 s was never reproduced. The table in the readme's "what was measured" section is honest, but one sentence under it should answer the owner's question directly.

`Server/TrackingCheck.mjs:155` builds `by_raw` with a Map. When two rows have the same raw text, the Map keeps the last one, but `PromptRecords.rid()` (`Server/PromptRecords.mjs:111`) uses `find` and keeps the first. The readme says replayed copies create exactly those duplicate raw rows, so check 4 can pick a different id than `PromptRecords --dry` does. Building the map so the first row wins (skip a key that is already set) keeps the two in step.

The readme's prompt-count paragraph gives e00f55c9 as 111 unique prompts and 131 raw lines, "all with parts". The committed `report.json` gives 122 unique, 97 with parts and 144 log lines, because the session kept growing after the backfill. Say that the paragraph's numbers are from the backfill, so a reader comparing it with the page isn't confused.
The page tail (`ext/JSONL` `live()`) is still not measured, and the browser number covers only the fetch and the parse. The readme says both plainly, which meets the fallback the brief allowed.
No screenshots came with this review. The minion reports opening the page headless at 1280 and 3440 and fixing two column overlaps, but I could not check the five-card row or tables 4 and 5 myself.

`review/diff.patch` is one commit behind the branch: it ends at 9533a26db, where `Server/TrackingCheck.mjs:156` sets `rid` and `missing` inside the `if` (a ReferenceError in strict ESM). Branch head b92e334a8 declares them on their own line (`TrackingCheck.mjs:182`). All three files pass `node --check`. Review the head, not the patch.

On the unmerged branch, `Servex/agents/page_tools.js` does not read `SERVEX_PUBLIC`. So `node Server/JsonlPerf.mjs --item` run without `TRACKING_ROOT` writes a probe record into the real tree at `public/framework/ai/sessions/zz-jsonlperf/session.jsonl`, and `clean()` never removes it. Merging (not cherry-picking) brings in michael/dev's `page_tools.js:12`, which fixes this. A one-line guard in `JsonlPerf.mjs:57` that refuses when `page_tools.js` has no `SERVEX_PUBLIC` would make it safe on any checkout.

The owner's core question, where the 60 s goes, is still not answered. No layer came close: the worst was 4.8 s. Every number was taken on code that already has the fast write (fbb4ca7d4), and the readme says this plainly (`public/framework/ai/tracking/readme.md`, last paragraph). A simpler way to reproduce it: run `JsonlPerf --item --source <e00f55c9 deputy record>` with `TRACKING_ROOT` set to a throwaway worktree at `fbb4ca7d4^`.

`--item` times the largest `session.jsonl` it finds (`2026/09/17/mastermind-layout-browser`, 397 KB), not the record the owner named (the e00f55c9 deputy record, 186 KB). `--source` exists, but nobody used it for the owner's file.

The 4,816 ms first write over HTTP appears only in the readme table. In `report.json`, `perf.http` is `null`, so the page's write table shows only the in-process 36–47 ms writes, and card 5's "slowest write seen" understates what was measured.
